## Context and Scope

The cliché has held for decades: when inflation rises, the advice is always the same — buy gold. That advice was put under the strongest test in forty years in 2022, when Headline CPI hit double digits across most of the OECD, surged past 100% in several emerging economies, and the gold price began the climb that would carry it past \$3,000 per ounce in 2024.

The project takes a single question seriously:

> **When inflation hit in 2022, who actually bought the gold?**

The question is deliberately phrased as a whodunit. The conventional answer — *consumers in high-inflation countries, hedging their savings* — is something the project's joined UN Comtrade + World Bank inflation dataset can either confirm or disconfirm at the country-year level. As the data report and the narrative-design document show, **the data disconfirms it**. The countries with the highest 2022 inflation (Venezuela, Lebanon, Sudan, Zimbabwe) imported almost no gold; the largest importers (Switzerland, China, the UAE, the UK, India) were almost all low-inflation economies. The project's central reveal sits in one country's data: **China's gold imports doubled in 2022, the same year Russia's foreign reserves were frozen by the G7**.

The final product is a single-page scrollytelling narrative, built in Streamlit, that walks a reader through this argument in five beats. The full beat-by-beat design is documented in `docs/narrative_design.md`. A Phase-1 diagnosis of the earlier dashboard-style draft and why it was scrapped is in `docs/diagnosis.md`.

## Project Objectives and Success Criteria

The objectives below are written as **story** outcomes, not as inventory checklists. They are derived from the personas in §3 and from the Bewertungsraster rubric criteria 4 (*Konsistenz mit Projektzielen und Bedürfnissen der Zielgruppe(n)*) and 5 (*Verständlichkeit*).

- **Drive a reader through one argument in under five minutes.** The reader should understand the central question within 30 seconds and leave with a one-sentence answer they can repeat the next day.
- **Make the disconfirmation visible.** A reader who scrolls past Beat 2 should *see*, on the chart, that high-inflation countries did not buy gold in 2022.
- **Land the political-economy reveal in Beat 4.** The China doubling and its 2022 context (Russian reserve freeze, World Gold Council's record 1,136 tons of central-bank purchases) should be legible from the chart and its annotations, without the reader needing to read the prose first.
- **Commit to a position.** The verdict (Beat 5) is a single, defensible claim — *gold's safe haven is now the sovereign's, not the citizen's* — supported by three specific numbers.
- **Stay reproducible.** Every visible number in the app traces to either the joined dataset described in the Data Report or to an explicit external citation (World Gold Council). No invented insights.

### Success Criteria

The earlier draft of this Charta listed criteria that measured *ingredients* ("≥ 4 chart types"). Those have been replaced with criteria that measure whether the story works:

| Criterion | How we measure it |
|---|---|
| Driving question is understood in 30 s | Heuristic check on Beat 1 + first lede paragraph |
| Disconfirmation is visible without prose | Beat 2 chart must show the inflation/imports gap on its own |
| One-sentence retention | Reader test (informal, n ≈ 3) on Verdict block |
| Source-traceable numbers | Every number in the app is either in the dataset or has an inline citation |
| Reproducibility | `uv sync && uv run streamlit run deployment/app.py` works from a clean clone |
| Variety + dataset size (rubric carry-over) | 4 chart types, 2017–2024 panel, ≥ 50 000 rows, 6+ categorical / numerical columns |

### Out of Scope

Price prediction, investment advice, real-time data, individual-investor analysis, and any analysis of ETF or jewellery demand are all out of scope. We are looking at **physical gold imports across borders, country-year, 2017–2024**. The dataset has a documented break at 2017 (see Data Report §4); the visible story respects that break and does not cross it.

## Stakeholder Analysis

The VDSS instructors are the primary client and assessor — they set the evaluation criteria, run coaching sessions, and assign the grade. The project team of three is responsible for all deliverables while running this alongside seven other modules. ZHAW peers attend the final presentation but have no influence on the grade. After publication, the website may attract a broader audience of finance-curious individuals and professionals, though they have no active role in the project.

In terms of influence and interest: the team sits highest on both axes since they do all the work and care most about the outcome. The instructors have high influence but are more distant from day-to-day decisions. Peers and the general public are low influence across the board.

## User Analysis

### Persona 1 — Lena Meier (24), Finance-Curious Student

Lena is a 3rd-semester Business Informatics student at ZHAW. She has CHF 5,000 to invest and keeps hearing from friends that gold is "the safest option" — but she's not sure whether to trust that. She has no formal finance training, reads basic charts fine but struggles with scatter plots and correlations, and uses her iPhone 14 as her primary device. She'd visit the website once or twice, explore a bit, maybe share something.

Jobs: understand whether gold is a sensible investment for someone without much capital; be able to talk about it with friends using real data; feel confident she's making an informed decision rather than just following social media.

Pains: financial articles are full of jargon; professional tools like Bloomberg feel overwhelming; she can't tell neutral analysis from gold seller marketing; charts she finds online are static and don't let her filter for her own country.

Gains: a clear visual answer written for non-experts; interactive features she can explore at her own pace; a concrete verdict at the end she can actually remember.

### Persona 2 — Thomas Brunner (52), Independent Financial Advisor

Thomas runs his own wealth advisory practice in Zürich. He has 20+ years of experience and has recommended a 5–10% gold allocation to clients for years — but he wants neutral, data-backed evidence to support that, not ETF brochures. He reads NZZ and Bloomberg daily, is comfortable with complex charts, and works desktop-first with PowerPoint for client presentations.

Jobs: find country-level evidence that gold acts as an inflation hedge; extract specific numbers for client slides; show clients something credible and neutral.

Pains: ETF marketing material is too biased to use with clients; academic papers are full of regression tables clients can't follow; most online visualizations are either too simple or too overwhelming; country-level trade flow data is hard to find.

Gains: well-designed neutral charts he can screenshot into PowerPoint; a country filter to highlight markets his clients care about; clear information about data sources so he can answer methodology questions on the spot.

## Situation Assessment

### Data

Dataset 1 — UN Global Commodity Trade Statistics (Kaggle): ~8.2M rows total, filtered to precious metals (HS codes 7106–7112) gives roughly 10,000–50,000 rows. Period: 1988–2016. Key variables: country, commodity, flow direction (import/export), trade value in USD, weight in kg, year.

Dataset 2 — World Bank Global Inflation Database (Ha, Kose & Ohnsorge, 2023): ~50,000 rows after reshaping (209 countries × 6 inflation types × 55 years). Period: 1970–2025. Key variables: country, country code, inflation type (Headline CPI, Food CPI, Energy CPI, Core CPI, PPI, GDP Deflator), economy type (Advanced / Emerging / Low-Income), year, inflation rate.

The combined dataset joined on country and year will have 6 categorical and 4 numerical variables — well above the course minimums.

### Team and Tools

Three team members, each contributing roughly 4–6 hours per week over ~10 weeks. Tools: Python (Pandas, NumPy) for data processing, Quarto for the website, Plotly and Streamlit for charts and GitHub for version control and deployment.

### Constraints and Risks

The project runs alongside 7 other modules, so available time per person is limited. The UN trade data ends in 2016, which means the 2022–2023 inflation spike can't be analyzed through trade flows. Any non-standard tools beyond what was introduced in lectures need justification.

| Risk | Likelihood | Mitigation |
|---|---|---|
| UN dataset too large to process locally | Medium | Filter to precious metals HS codes immediately; use chunked Pandas reading if needed |
| Country name mismatches between datasets | High | Join on ISO-3166 codes, not names; build a manual mapping table early |
| Scrollytelling harder to implement than expected | Medium | Fallback: standard Quarto site with static Plotly charts — still meets all requirements |
| Time pressure from parallel modules | High | Buffer week at end of schedule; cut nice-to-haves before cutting core visualizations |
| Uneven work distribution | Low | Clear roles from week 1; transparent commit history on GitHub |

## Visualization Concept

The product is a single-page scrollytelling narrative built in Streamlit. The reader's only control is the scroll wheel; there is no sidebar, no global filter, and no widget inside the narrative. State changes are bound to scroll position. Visual emphasis (a 2022 highlight, a China bar, a Venezuela near-zero) is hard-coded by the author, not by the reader.

The five beats below replace the earlier draft's five chapters. The full visual specification — colour, axis, annotation — lives in `viz_design_report.qmd`; what follows is the narrative role of each beat.

**Beat 1 — Buy gold.**
A line chart of global gold imports from 2017 to 2024. Only the 2022 point is highlighted; the rest of the line is muted. An on-chart annotation calls out the \$541 B figure ("the year inflation peaked"). The beat sets up the safe-haven cliché so the next beat can break it.

**Beat 2 — But not in Caracas.**
A hand-curated horizontal bar chart of 11 countries — six high-inflation (Venezuela, Lebanon, Sudan, Zimbabwe, Argentina, Iran) and five low-inflation (Switzerland, China, UAE, India, UK). Y-axis sorted by 2022 Headline CPI; X-axis is gold imports in USD millions. The high-inflation countries have invisible bars; the low-inflation countries have huge ones. The visual disconfirms the consumer-inflation story without the prose needing to do the work.

**Beat 3 — Then who?**
A ranked bar chart of the top eight 2022 gold importers, coloured by Headline CPI. The reader sees that four of the top five had inflation below 6%. The beat closes the door on the consumer reading and opens the next question.

**Beat 4 — China doubled down.**
A bar chart of China's gold imports, 2017–2024. The 2022 bar is highlighted; on-chart annotations call out the COVID-2020 collapse and the 2022 +116% jump, with the latter explicitly framed as coinciding with the G7 freeze of Russian foreign reserves. The 1,136-ton World Gold Council central-bank purchase figure (the highest since 1950) appears in the chart caveat as an external citation.

**Beat 5 — The verdict.**
A three-number recap (+116 % / ≈ \$0 / 1,136 t) followed by one sentence: *gold's safe-haven role is alive — it is just no longer the citizen's hedge against inflation, but the sovereign's hedge against the dollar*. No new chart. The numbers are the chart.
